_comment: A plain-language line for each requirement listed, shown beside its framework's own words in the report, never in place of them (backlog 0372). Written for ASVS 5.0's level-1 requirements first. Read through sv_frameworks::data; held to each requirement's own words by crates/sv-report/tests/plain_requirements.rs.

plain.V1.2.1: Text the app puts into a page, a header, or an XML document is encoded for the exact place it goes, so it cannot change the page's structure.
plain.V1.2.2: Untrusted data put into a web address is encoded for where it goes in the address, and only safe kinds of address (never javascript: or data:) are allowed.
plain.V1.2.3: Untrusted data put into JavaScript or JSON the app builds is encoded or escaped, so it cannot change the script's or the JSON's structure.
plain.V1.2.4: Database queries keep the data apart from the query itself (parameterized queries, an ORM, or something as safe), so nobody can inject their own query.
plain.V1.2.5: The app never lets input become part of an operating-system command: commands are given their arguments separately, or the input is encoded for the command line.
plain.V1.3.1: HTML that people write in a rich-text editor is cleaned with a well-known, secure HTML sanitizing library or framework feature before it is used.
plain.V1.3.2: The app does not run text as code (eval, SpEL, and the like); where there is truly no alternative, any user input in it is sanitized first.
plain.V1.5.1: XML parsers are set up restrictively, with dangerous features such as external entities turned off, so XML cannot be used for an XXE attack.
plain.V2.1.1: The app's documentation says what valid data looks like for each kind of input: an email address, a phone number, a card number, or the app's own formats.
plain.V2.2.1: Input is checked against what the app expects (allowed values, patterns, ranges, or structure); at level 1, at least the input used to make business or security decisions.
plain.V2.2.2: Input is validated on the server, the trusted side; checks in the browser help people but are never relied on for security.
plain.V2.3.1: A multi-step process, such as a checkout, runs its steps in order for the same user, and no step can be skipped.
plain.V3.2.1: The browser cannot be tricked into showing a response in the wrong context, such as an API response or an uploaded file opened directly as a page.
plain.V3.2.2: Content meant to be shown as text is put on the page with safe functions (such as textContent), so it can never run as HTML or JavaScript.
plain.V3.3.1: Cookies have the Secure attribute, so they are only sent over HTTPS, and their names use the __Host- or __Secure- prefix.
plain.V3.4.1: Every response tells browsers to use only HTTPS for this site (the Strict-Transport-Security header), for at least a year.
plain.V3.4.2: Cross-origin access (CORS) is allowed only for a fixed origin or origins on an allowlist; when any origin is allowed, the response holds nothing sensitive.
plain.V3.5.1: Requests that do something sensitive are checked to come from the app itself (with an anti-forgery token or a special header), to stop cross-site request forgery (CSRF), unless the CORS preflight already does that.
plain.V3.5.2: Where the app relies on the browser's CORS preflight to block other sites, sensitive actions cannot be reached by a request that skips the preflight.
plain.V3.5.3: Sensitive actions use POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, never GET or another method meant to be safe, or the request's Sec-Fetch headers are checked strictly instead.
plain.V4.1.1: Every response with a body says what kind of content it is (the Content-Type header) and matches it, including the character set, such as UTF-8.
plain.V4.4.1: Every WebSocket connection is encrypted (wss://, WebSocket over TLS).
plain.V5.2.1: The app accepts only files small enough to process without slowing down or being knocked over.
plain.V5.2.2: An uploaded file's extension is one the app expects, and its contents really are that type (checking its first bytes, for example); at level 1, at least files used for business or security decisions.
plain.V5.3.1: Files that people upload into a public folder can never be run as code on the server when someone opens their address.
plain.V5.3.2: File paths are built from names the app makes or trusts, not names people send; if a user's file name must be used, it is strictly checked, so nobody can reach other files or servers.
plain.V6.1.1: The documentation says how the app defends sign-in against password guessing and stolen-password lists (rate limiting and the like), how that is set up, and how it avoids locking real users out.
plain.V6.2.1: Passwords people choose are at least 8 characters long; at least 15 is strongly recommended.
plain.V6.2.3: Changing a password asks for the current password as well as the new one.
plain.V6.2.4: A new or changed password is checked against at least the 3,000 most common passwords that fit the app's rules, and refused if it is one of them.
plain.V6.2.5: Passwords can contain any characters, with no rules demanding upper case, numbers, or symbols.
plain.V6.2.6: Password fields hide what is typed (type=password); the app may let people show it for a moment.
plain.V6.2.7: People can paste passwords and use the browser's or another password manager.
plain.V6.2.8: The password is checked exactly as typed, never cut short or changed to lower or upper case.
plain.V6.3.1: The defenses against password guessing and stolen-password lists are in place, as the app's documentation says they are.
plain.V6.3.2: There are no default accounts such as root, admin, or sa, or they are turned off.
plain.V6.4.1: First passwords and activation codes the system makes are random, follow the password rules, expire soon or after first use, and cannot be kept as the long-term password.
plain.V6.4.2: There are no password hints or secret questions.
plain.V7.2.1: Session tokens are checked on the server, the trusted side, every time.
plain.V7.2.2: Sessions use tokens made fresh for each session, never a fixed API key or secret.
plain.V7.2.3: Session tokens that point to data on the server are unique and made by a secure random generator, with at least 128 bits of randomness.
plain.V7.2.4: Signing in, or signing in again, gives a new session token and ends the old one.
plain.V7.4.1: Once a session ends (signing out, or it expires), it cannot be used again; the server forgets it, or self-contained tokens are refused after that point.
plain.V7.4.2: When an account is disabled or deleted, all of its active sessions end.
plain.V8.1.1: The documentation sets out who may use which functions, and who may see or change which records.
plain.V8.2.1: Each function can be used only by people who have been given permission for it.
plain.V8.2.2: Each record can be reached only by people who have been given permission for that record, so nobody can open someone else's by changing an id in the address.
plain.V8.3.1: Who may do what is enforced on the server, never by things a user could change, such as hidden buttons or JavaScript in the browser.
plain.V9.1.1: A self-contained token, such as a JWT, has its signature checked before anything in it is trusted.
plain.V9.1.2: Self-contained tokens can be made and checked only with algorithms on an allowlist, never the 'none' algorithm.
plain.V9.1.3: The keys used to check self-contained tokens come only from trusted sources set up in advance, never from a source named inside the token.
plain.V9.2.1: A token is accepted only within its validity period; for a JWT, its nbf and exp times are checked.
plain.V10.4.1: The authorization server accepts only redirect addresses registered in advance for each client, compared exactly.
plain.V10.4.2: An authorization code can be used only once; a second use is refused, and the tokens issued from it are revoked.
plain.V10.4.3: Authorization codes expire quickly: within 10 minutes at levels 1 and 2.
plain.V10.4.4: Each client may use only the grant types it needs, and never the implicit ('token') or the 'password' grant.
plain.V10.4.5: Refresh tokens for public clients cannot be replayed: they are tied to the client, or rotated so a used one is refused and its family revoked.
plain.V11.3.1: Insecure encryption modes such as ECB, and weak padding such as PKCS#1 v1.5, are not used.
plain.V11.3.2: Only approved ciphers and modes, such as AES with GCM, are used.
plain.V11.4.1: Only approved hash functions are used for cryptography; MD5 and the like are never used for any cryptographic purpose.
plain.V12.1.1: Only the latest recommended TLS versions, such as 1.2 and 1.3, are turned on, with the newest preferred.
plain.V12.2.1: All connections from clients to the app's public web services use TLS, and never fall back to unencrypted connections.
plain.V12.2.2: The app's public services use TLS certificates that browsers trust.
plain.V13.4.1: The app is deployed without its source control folders (.git, .svn), or they cannot be reached, from outside or by the app itself.
plain.V14.2.1: Sensitive data, such as an API key or a session token, is sent only in the body or the headers of a request, never in the web address.
plain.V14.3.1: Signed-in data is cleared from the browser when the session ends, even when the server cannot be reached.
plain.V15.1.1: The documentation sets deadlines for fixing third-party components with known weaknesses, and for keeping libraries up to date, by how risky they are.
plain.V15.2.1: Every component the app ships is within the update and fix deadlines its documentation sets.
plain.V15.3.1: The app returns only the fields of a record that are needed, never the whole record with fields some users must not see.
